title: Learned MRI brain-age gap associates with cognition and disability in geriatric depression
summary: A pretrained convolutional brain-age estimator was applied without retuning to midlife and older-adult cohorts totaling 170 and 154 participants, respectively. Older depressed adults had a higher estimated-minus-chronological age gap than older controls, with associations to poorer episodic memory and greater disability. Comparable diagnosis and cognition associations were not observed in the midlife cohort. This cross-sectional, exploratory analysis estimates an MRI-derived age difference; it does not measure an individual’s longitudinal aging rate or demonstrate that depression causes accelerated aging. Differences between cohort protocols and the need for replication constrain interpretation.
organization: Vanderbilt University Medical Center; Vanderbilt University; Veterans Affairs Tennessee Valley Health System

evidence.tested: MRI-derived brain-age estimates in 170 midlife and 154 older participants; cognitive associations in both cohorts and disability assessment in the older group. Model pretrained on over 5,000 healthy controls.
evidence.unknown: Cross-sectional associations, separate cohort protocols and exploratory subgroup tests. No causal aging trajectory, clinical predictive utility or independent confirmation established.
evidence.ai_role: A pretrained convolutional regression model converted MRI/anatomical features into estimated brain age, enabling comparison of age-gap relationships across depression/age cohorts.

source_review.scope: Independent full primary Abstract, participants, brain-age inference and analytic Methods, Results and Discussion limitations; actual publisher date/affiliations. No supplement review.
